title: Secret Lakes Under the Red Sea Are Full of Tiny Life
summary:
More than a mile under the Red Sea, scientists found lakes. But these are not normal lakes: the water is so salty no fish can live in it. Still, tiny living things called microbes live there.

The lakes are called brine pools. Scientists from the University of Miami found them in the Gulf of Aqaba, part of the Red Sea. A robot submarine found them 1,770 meters down, in the last five minutes of a ten-hour dive. 'We were very lucky,' said Sam Purkis.

The water in brine pools is very salty and has no oxygen at all. Studying the microbes there may help scientists learn how far life can go on Earth, and help them look for life on other planets. Some molecules from these microbes may even help fight cancer.

The pools also keep clues about the past. Their salty water saves traces of old tsunamis, floods, and earthquakes. In 2022, the team found signs of a 500-year-old landslide that probably caused a big tsunami. This could help plan for coastal towns in Egypt and Saudi Arabia.
why_it_matters: Learning how tiny life survives in such harsh places could one day lead to new medicines that help sick people, including kids like you.

background_read: Brine pools are lakes of very salty water that sit on the sea floor, in deep parts of the sea.
Their water is so salty and has no oxygen at all, so no fish can live there, but tiny microbes can.
Scientists send robot submarines down to find these hidden pools and learn how life can survive in such harsh places.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists from the University of Miami, including Sam Purkis, and the tiny microbes living in the pools.
WHAT: They found hidden lakes of super-salty water called brine pools deep under the Red Sea, full of tiny microbes.
WHERE: In the Gulf of Aqaba, part of the Red Sea, 1,770 meters down.
WHY: To learn how far life can go on Earth, look for life on other planets, and use clues in the pools to plan for coastal towns.
